items.title: Cascadeability and the Realization Gap: An Empirical Study of LLM-Powered Semantic Filtering
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic filters enable natural language predicates over unstructured documents, but evaluating every document with a large language model (LLM) oracle is expensive. Proxy cascades reduce oracle invocations using cheaper surrogates, but oracle reduction alone cannot distinguish proxy limitations from calibration bottlenecks and establish practical efficiency. We present a unified benchmark of four representative systems, which formulate query processing as a three-stage workflow comprising proxy construction, threshold calibration, and cascade inference, using a two-threshold acceptance rule. We introduce cascadeability: the maximum empirical oracle reduction attainable from fixed proxy scores at a specified accuracy target, computed retrospectively using complete oracle labels. We investigate 8 research questions, spanning proxy quality, end-to-end performance, workload sensitivities, and component ablations, and reveal our key findings accordingly. Comparing cascadeability with achieved oracle reduction yields a realization gap that, interpreted alongside accuracy, exposes distinct proxy and calibration bottlenecks. The benchmark and diagnostics support evaluation beyond oracle reduction and motivate joint proxy-calibration design, class-sensitive quality assessment, and end-to-end cost optimization. We release a dataset-query benchmark, containing 10 real-world workloads across various domains and difficulties, with annotations of two LLM families.

items.title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.

items.title: Exploring Agentic Visual Analytics: A Co-Evolutionary Framework of Roles and Workflows
items.summary: arXiv:2604.15813v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic visual analytics (VA) represents an emerging class of systems in which large language model (LLM)-driven agents autonomously plan, execute, evaluate, and iterate across the full visual analytics pipeline. By shifting users from low-level tool operations to high-level analytical goals expressed through natural language, these systems are fundamentally transforming how humans interact with data. However, the rapid proliferation of such systems in recent years has outpaced our understanding of their design landscape. Two intertwined problems remain open: how do autonomous agents reshape the traditional VA pipeline, and how must human involvement adapt as agent autonomy increases? To address these questions, this paper presents a comprehensive survey of 55 primary agentic VA systems and introduces a co-evolutionary framework. This framework is essential because it jointly analyzes the progression of agent autonomy alongside the necessary shift in human roles from manual operators to strategic supervisors. Within this framework, we define a role-workflow taxonomy that aligns four key agentic roles (PLANNER, CREATOR, REVIEWER, and CONTEXT MANAGER) and maps them onto established VA pipeline stages. Our analysis uncovers recurring trade-offs along three foundational axes: autonomy levels, agentic roles, and the VA workflow. We consolidate these findings into actionable design guidelines and outline future research directions for agentic visual analytics. A web-based interactive browser of our co-evolutionary framework, including the corpus and design guidelines, is available at agenticva.github.io/AgenticVA/.

items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

items.title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

items.title: ProvCards: Artifact-Oriented Provenance for Heterogeneous Scientific Workflows
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducibility in scientific workflows is hindered by heterogeneous components and execution environments, as well as fragmented provenance capture. Although existing approaches offer established semantics and workflow-specific solutions, provenance remains difficult to capture, exchange, and compose across workflow boundaries. We present ProvCards, an artifact-oriented approach that treats provenance as a first-class artifact grounded in the W3C PROV Data Model. Individual workflow components can generate cards that are stored, exchanged, reused, and composed independently of any workflow system or centralized execution context. ProvDecks group related cards into portable scopes while preserving their identities. ProvGraphs provide derived views for provenance reconstruction, querying, visualization, and analysis. Together, these representations support coherent, task-specific provenance views across heterogeneous components, facilitating traceability, reuse, and reproducibility. We implement ProvCards using a graph-based infrastructure and evaluate them in a scientific data-processing workflow. The results demonstrate independent provenance capture at the component level, composition across component boundaries, and reconstruction for querying and analysis. ProvCards provide a portable, composable, and incrementally extensible foundation for provenance management in heterogeneous scientific workflows.

items.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

items.title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

items.title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

items.title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.
